#192289. What’s a Vintage Car Rally Really Like? Inside the Louis Vuitton Dolomites Classic Run.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1013 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

What’s a Vintage Car Rally Really Like? Inside the Louis Vuitton Dolomites Classic Run.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in vintage rally driving, there are generally two types of competitor.
  • It has been revealed that gianandrea Redaelli, a car nut whose family has long roots in the Italian printing business, is firmly in the “road book” camp.
  • In a recent development, venice might not seem the most logical starting line for a car rally given the proverbial wetness of the streets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in vintage rally driving, there are generally two types of competitor. Both share a passion for keeping priceless and nearly century-old vehicles in use on the open road rather than displaying them under glass. But some see the drive itself as challenge enough, while stalwarts adhere to what’s called the road book. This is a hundred or so pages of complex navigational directions that the copilot uses to navigate instead of a map, maintaining a constant flow of instructions to the driver. It is this book and how closely you follow it that decides the eventual winner.

It has been revealed that gianandrea Redaelli, a car nut whose family has long roots in the Italian printing business, is firmly in the “road book” camp. In early September, I climbed into the copilot seat of his 1939 Aston Martin C-Type Speed Model Roadster Bertelli—just one of two ever built, with an experimental aerodynamic body that earned it the nickname “the Flying Pea”—and stayed there as he drove six hundred kilometers of “left at the traffic lights, right at the cow” for the Louis Vuitton Dolomites Classic Run. The rally started in Venice and ended, after a scenic but challenging detour high into the Dolomite mountains, at Monza, the home of Italian Formula 1, just in time for practice day of the Grand Prix.

In a recent development, venice might not seem the most logical starting line for a car rally given the proverbial wetness of the streets. But the city was chosen this year because it was also the end point of the last LV rally of its kind: the La Serenissima Run from Monte Carlo to Venice in 2012. Gianandrea won that one as copilot, with his father, Giuseppe, at the wheel. The pair also won the one before it—the Boheme across Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Austria—in 2006. This time, however, the pressure was on me too.

I have been a copilot before, and I can tell you it’s no picnic. Rally racing in vintage cars is less about speed and more about timing. It’s an exercise that requires pinpoint accuracy at the time-stamp points in the overall course and, most critically, in the regularities. These are fiendishly short time-over-distance sections in which crossing the line just a few hundredths of a second late—or early—earns strict penalties. Sensibly, the day before the race began, Gianandrea took me out in the Aston in the Veneto countryside to practice, especially those critical regularities.

I could have opted for an easy life. The rally allowed competing cars, dating from 1931 to 1969, to use the road book or follow the course using a map in a dedicated phone app. But where’s the fun in that?

“If you join a competition, you follow the regulations and strive to do your best,” Gianandrea says. “As an Italian, if you paint numbers on the door of my car, I will want to win.”.

Industry observers note that every car in a rally like this comes with its own idiosyncrasies. On flat ground, someone driving a souped-up 2026 sports car would find these tests difficult to nail. In the reality of race conditions, the regularities often involve steep climbs or descents and unexpected corners, alling for an expert hand at the wheel—and foot on the gas pedal. The tendency of some car doors to swing open at hard bends (ours has the “suicide” doors with hinges on the back instead of the front, beloved by early carmakers) only adds to the excitement. The purpose of driver and copilot is to battle and overcome all the mechanical and computational challenges—and get our ride to the finish line bang on time.

Louis Vuitton has been involved in these glamorous and exacting vintage rallies since 1993. The Dolomites Run represents an enthusiastic return to the genre after a fourteen-year gap and, perhaps tellingly, the manufacturer’s global sponsorship (since 2025) of Formula 1. Unconfirmed rumors circulated in the field that the choice of ending the rally at a Grand Prix could well be repeated—and soon—in other countries in the future.

It’s easy, after all, to see why a fusion of style and cars with six- and seven-figure price tags might appeal to Louis Vuitton and competitors alike. Not surprisingly, at every coffee and lunch stop, the LV effect sprinkled the race with an added sense of luxury. In between, our snaking caravan carried the glamour of a century of motoring along with it. At every hairpin you got a glimpse of a gull-wing Mercedes, a 1931 Bugatti two-seater (my personal fave), and a shimmering behemoth of a Bentley in quick succession. These cars would turn heads anywhere. But in Italy, arguably the home of the sports car, they brought smiles, applause, and gasps in even the tiniest village that passed by in our slipstream. I swear I even saw a nun with a glint in her eye at one set of traffic lights.

Industry observers note that navigating, I was rapidly learning, is not so much about providing a constant babble of information as it is knowing how to give clear and simple instructions—and only when strictly needed. As the finish neared in Monza at the end of two long days on the road, I was able to give Gianandrea the most helpful instruction of all: “Nothing for 15 kilometers.”.

“That,” he very kindly replied, “is the mark of a pro.”.

Even after the engines cooled, we were still clueless about how well we’d done overall. That changed at the final event, a dinner inside the Sforzesco Castle in Milan. Gianandrea stepped up, beaming, as winner of the race, and for the first time as driver. I stood somewhat sheepishly behind him as copilot as he received the trophy from Pietro Beccari, CEO of both Louis Vuitton and Louis Vuitton Fashion Group. It was an impressive swirl of Murano glass created by Venini, housed in its own equally impressive traveling case, made (naturellement) at Louis Vuitton’s atelier in Asnières.

Gianandrea has promised me visiting rights.

#192284. Does Anyone Care How Yellowjackets Ends Anymore?

Does Anyone Care How Yellowjackets Ends Anymore?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Believe it or not, Yellowjackets is based on real events.
  • Yellowjackets, in a way, explores what might have happened had the group never revealed just how they managed to survive in the wilderness.
  • In a recent development, the series explored survival in all its forms, from the lasting effects of grief to the need for women to escape their mundane, suburban lives for a little danger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Believe it or not, Yellowjackets is based on real events. In 1972, a high school rugby team, along with their families, boarded Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571 and crashed in the Andes. Only sixteen of the forty-five passengers survived when they were rescued seventy-two days later, and they all harbored a dark secret: To survive, they ate the flesh of the people who had died.

Yellowjackets, in a way, explores what might have happened had the group never revealed just how they managed to survive in the wilderness. Much like Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571, the Showtime series follows a high school women’s soccer team that survives a plane crash by killing and eating each other. Cocreators Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson blended in potential supernatural elements such as a dark presence that possibly forces them to kill, classic Lord of the Flies homages, and a killer soundtrack. Yellowjackets also cut ahead to each survivor’s life as an adult, featuring the acting talents of Melanie Lynskey, Christina Ricci, and Juliette Lewis. For a while, it was engrossing TV.

In a recent development, the series explored survival in all its forms, from the lasting effects of grief to the need for women to escape their mundane, suburban lives for a little danger. It was critically acclaimed, nominated for awards, and topped many “Best of the Year” lists. But then, five years and two more chaotic seasons went by that really seemed to test its audience’s … well, appetites.

According to recent reports, now that the fourth and final season is upon us—season 4 premiered on Friday, November 20—the answers to Yellowjackets’ burning questions will finally be revealed. Namely: Is something forcing them to kill each other, or can everything be explained by science? Will the public find out that they resorted to ritualistic murder and cannibalism? And, most importantly, is there anyone left who’s still interested in finding out?

To be fair, there’s already something of an answer to that last question. Despite critical fatigue for the series, over two million viewers tuned in to the season 3 premiere last year, per Paramount. That number then increased a bit to 3 million by the season 3 finale. Sure, those numbers pale in comparison to The Pitt season 2’s 15.4 million average weekly viewers or even the Landman season 2 premiere’s 9.2 million viewers. But there is a fan base willing to see this series to the end, whatever happens.

What is that ending? Where the series presently stands, our girls are finally returning home after being rescued. They’ll likely adjust to normal life again by committing another hunt back in their hometown. And in the present, the promise of “last one standing” in the pre-roll recap likely points to a final bloodbath. Is that even what fans want? Until that finale, how everything will resolve, and what it all really means, remains a mystery.

For the Uruguayans, they faced a moral and religious crisis when they returned. When news broke that the rugby team ate the flesh of their dead passengers, one of the survivors defended their actions by comparing it to that of Jesus Christ and the Eucharist. According to the survivor, the group made a pact to sacrifice their bodies for each other if they perished so that they could eat their flesh to survive. The media circus completely flipped, and they were heroes once again. Pope Paul VI even wrote them a letter to sanctify their actions. It’s a fascinating end to their story—but one that the Yellowjackets cocreators likely found made for an entirely different sort of TV show.

Outside of the pagan imagery and supernatural threats that the Yellowjackets cast face, religion has yet to enter the picture. The cannibalism mostly seemed inevitable until it finally happened halfway through season 2, and besides that, the women have done much worse since returning home. After three seasons of one cold-blooded murder after another, the body count just to keep their secret hidden is enough for all of them to face the electric chair. And even if there is a malevolent force controlling them, it may take a metaphorical release of pain and grief on par with Hereditary or Weapons to fully satisfy viewers in the series finale.

“To some extent, I do feel as though if we were to just 100 percent jump both feet on one side of [the supernatural/reality] line, it would disperse some of what makes this show interesting,” cocreator Ashley Lyle told CBR ahead of season 4.

Recent findings suggest that “I think that we are fully aware that we are either going to delight or anger both sides of that equation in some way, shape, or form,” they added. “But I don’t know that that could have been avoided.”.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, some version of watching the women all kill each other, or even watching them all defeat the evil they believe is haunting them, just doesn’t feel like enough. The show’s biggest problem might have just been that it ran too long. A simpler ending to a shorter story might have left viewers delighted. But we shall see! If Yellowjackets can land the plane (sorry) in the end, I’m willing to eat (apologies again) my own words on this one.

Industry News: 7 Holiday Decor Trends Designers Say We're About to See Everywhere

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pictured above: A holiday-ready space by designer Marie Flanigan.
  • Christmas is just around the corner, and as the holiday spirit makes its way into our homes, it’s a good time to give your seasonal decor a refresh.
  • However, if you’re in the mood to try something a little different, here are seven trends on our radar for a chic Christmas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pictured above: A holiday-ready space by designer Marie Flanigan.

Christmas is just around the corner, and as the holiday spirit makes its way into our homes, it’s a good time to give your seasonal decor a refresh. This year, on-trend doesn’t have to mean brand-new—designers love decorating with heirloom pieces collected over time.

However, if you’re in the mood to try something a little different, here are seven trends on our radar for a chic Christmas.

Industry observers note that this winter, our decor is taking a note from European culture—again. Swedish folk art is emerging as a hot winter trend in both holiday and home decor. Defined by bold red hues, tulip motifs, and S-scrolls, the style blends cozy-core with the heritage style craze.

“European folk influences are so significant right now,” claims designer Johanna Lyle of Jo Lyle & Co. “Think Swedish Dala horses, quilt motifs, and decorative stitching. I think we will see those continue into holiday decor.”.

In a recent development, when it comes to her tree decor, interior designer Francesca Grace waves a hand at the carefully contrived, and she’s not alone. “My ornaments are collected from my travels, so the tree is really a collection of memories. I love unpacking them and remembering where each one came from. They don’t all match, and I wouldn’t want them to,” says Grace. “I let the ornaments lead. That mix feels much more personal to me, and it gives the tree something new to say as the collection grows.” This year’s trends hinge on antiqued, inherited style, with one-off pieces that channel bold character and hardly ever come with a matching set.

Interior designer Marie Flanigan likes to add a fresh twist to her seasonal decor with dried oranges and pops of cranberry red.

In a recent development, “We've seen such a beautiful resurgence of dried citrus in holiday decorating over the past few years,” Flanigan explains. “And I think cranberries are ready for their moment to shine. Their rich red hue feels especially festive, and I love the idea of incorporating them into fresh greenery, draping them across a mantel, or pairing them with dried oranges for a more layered look.”.

If there’s one classic Christmas element Grace hopes makes a comeback, it's multicolored lights. Inherently nostalgic, these bold-hued bulbs were a ’90s staple.

Sources indicate that “I’m ready for a little less restraint on the tree. Those reds, blues, greens, and yellows immediately bring back the feeling of Christmas as a child. They also pull together a collection of ornaments that might otherwise seem completely unrelated. White lights can be beautiful, but I want my Christmas tree to have some mischief,” says Grace.

The classic red-and-green combination may take the title for the most iconic holiday palette, but this year, color trends are going complementary. While base colors stay warm and slightly rusted, patterned pieces are taking on cooler tones. This year, we’re also trading traditional plaid for Scottish tartan.

“Warm crimsons, rich browns, tactile fabrics, and blue-green plaids make a beautiful holiday palette,” claims Elizabeth Bennett, cofounder of the interior design firm Kobel + Co.

In a total rejection of mass-manufactured everything, handmade felt pieces are taking holiday homes by storm. The style has even coined a newly introduced holiday aesthetic: #Kitschmas, and, according to Lyle, it’s here to stay. “As AI continues to homogenize design, things made by humans will feel more special and important. Handmade and crafted items create stories around decor that feel meaningful and can be treasured year after year,” she notes.

In a recent development, moody browns are steadily emerging as the latest neutral as we inch closer to the new year, and lucky for our winter design schemes, the hue really is as versatile as it seems. Paired with powdery blues, bold crimsons, and even minty greens, chocolate brown grounds nearly any palette and matches every metallic hue.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m particularly drawn to chocolate brown as an unexpected foundation for holiday color palettes. It's incredibly rich and versatile. I love the idea of moving beyond traditional red and green and allowing the existing colors of a room to inform the holiday decor. You can create something incredibly festive through tonal layering, subtle metallic accents, and variations in material,” Flanigan explains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that happy birthday, Hailey Bieber! The star has officially turned 30, and to mark another turn around the sun, she kicked off a week of celebrations with a latest navy-blue Rhode drop, a festive campaign, and an intimate video series that followed a week in her life. Throughout the vlogs, we saw the founder in fittings and makeup chairs, spending time with son Jack Blues, and reflecting on the past decade. “Becoming a mom definitely changed me the most in my twenties,” she told the camera. “I always knew I wanted to be a mom, I always knew I wanted kids, and it just totally transforms you as a person for the better.”.

In a recent development, of course, the birth-week celebrations have also come with a wardrobe to match. From shearling coats to archival statements, she ushered in the newly introduced season with everything from an ivory satin Oriori coat trimmed in gray-white fur to a black silk Armani Privé Fall 2005 set to a Yohji Yamamoto Spring 1998 jacket previously seen on Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy. And we did not expect anything less from the star.

Throughout the years, Bieber has become as known for her style as for her Rhode lipgloss phone cases, playing with understated “quiet luxury,” classic Los Angeles athleisure, and tons of Saint Laurent leather. As she grew from a teenage model into a business owner and, later, young mother, her taste has evolved over time—but through it all, she has given us some major fashion inspiration.

So, in honor of her 30th birthday, we rounded up our 30 favorite looks from the star. And between her plethora of Met Gala ensembles, polka-dot prints, and mismatched moments with husband Justin, there was a lot to pick from.

For the Fresh York Times Dealbook Summit, Bieber takes a page from Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy and wears a Yohji Yamamoto Spring 1998 jacket previously worn by the late It girl.

Stepping out in Fresh York City, Bieber pairs her Phoebe Philo cropped fur coat with blue jeans and vintage Manolos.

The star wears the coat of the season: Conner Ives’s reconstituted fur robe in white silk mikado.

Bieber wears an iridescent jacket from Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel Fall 2026 collection. With a medley of silver, red, and turquoise mesh, the piece puts an aluminum chainmail twist on the house’s signature tweed.

For the Academy Museum Gala, Bieber wears a custom bubblegum-pink Chanel dress.

At the 2026 Vanity Fair Oscar after-party, she hits the carpet wearing a shimmering leopard-print gown, made custom by Armani Privé. She accessorizes with Lorraine Schwartz jewelry and Manolo Blahnik heels.

While in Tokyo, Bieber wears a textured Issey Miyake egg-carton skirt suit from the Fall/Winter 2000 collection.

Doing press in Australia, Bieber wears a green Valentino Spring 2026 minidress, with structured shoulders, ruching, and a sweet bow at the hem.

Bieber attends the GQ Men Of The Year party in a naked dress and sparkly Gucci thong, bringing back the ’90s trend.

At the 2025 Academy Museum Gala, Bieber steps out in a striking, sculptural gown from Schiaparelli, constructed from brown moiré vintage ribbons for the house’s Spring/Summer 2025 Haute Couture runway.

Supporting Kylie Jenner at the Kylie Cosmetics anniversary event, Bieber looks to Wiederhoeft for a belted satin midi dress, designed with a chunky belt and thigh-high slit.

While out for an evening in Fresh York, Bieber turns heads in an electric green minidress from Dolce & Gabbana’s 2003 collection.

Stepping out in Fresh York, Bieber embraces two of the year's biggest trends—polka dots and capris—all in one go.

Bieber wears a Marine Serre dress made out of metallic-silver watch straps for a weekend in Miami during the Grand Prix.

Bieber spends an NYC evening at Cafe Zaffri, wearing a silky ice-blue minidress—a vintage Gucci piece from the fashion house’s Spring/Summer 1998 collection, designed by Tom Ford.

Leaving Funk in Los Angeles with Justin, Hailey is seen in an oversized gray suit with strong shoulders and baggy trousers, paired with a burgundy tie and matching clutch.

Stepping out with Justin, who matches his wife's Adidas with a pop of red, Hailey layers on the leopard print patterns—pairing a matching trench and shoulder bag from Saint Laurent.

Bieber highlights her bump with a silky white asymmetrical minidress and matching square-toe heels.

For her pregnancy announcement, Bieber poses in a bridal long-sleeve Saint Laurent maxi dress and matching lacy veil, with chunky sunglasses for a full old Hollywood glam look.

Captured in what have since become iconic photos, Hailey and Justin take couples dressing to new contrasting heights, with her in a little red dress and him in a gray hoodie and Crocs.

#192278. Dreaming of Buying a Home Abroad? These 10 Countries Make It Shockingly Simple

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1223 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

Dreaming of Buying a Home Abroad? These 10 Countries Make It Shockingly Simple

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that over the last few years, many Americans have daydreamed about life abroad.
  • It has been revealed that certain countries, like Australia, Canada, and New Zealand, have bans on foreign buyers.
  • Choosing the right location can make moving abroad much less intimidating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that over the last few years, many Americans have daydreamed about life abroad. Moving internationally can often feel like a pipe dream, but with the right planning, it’s possible. However, lengthy visa processes, daunting language barriers, and a difficult-to-navigate legal system can make the dream feel more like a nightmare.

It has been revealed that certain countries, like Australia, Canada, and New Zealand, have bans on foreign buyers. Others, like Thailand, Cuba, and Vietnam, don’t allow outsiders to own property at all. On the other end of the spectrum are countries actively trying to attract foreign buyers, offering enviable incentives like affordable home prices, a smoother customs process, and an easier-to-navigate work-visa approval process.

Choosing the right location can make moving abroad much less intimidating. Ahead, we’re breaking down the ten best countries for Americans looking to buy property abroad. Whether you’re dreaming of relocating or searching for your perfect vacation home, these countries make buying as easy as possible and offer gorgeous landscapes too.

Industry observers note that if you’ve ever dreamed of living among medieval architecture and rolling mountain ranges, Georgia might be the key to unlocking your fantasy. A bridge between Eastern Europe and Western Asia, the transcontinental country borders Russia, Turkey, Armenia, and the Black Sea, offering both subtropical and high-altitude climates. Thankfully, the real estate landscape is much less complex, with few legal or bureaucratic hurdles for American buyers, no residency or visa required (for up to a year), and remarkably fast processing times. In fact, the only major restriction in the Georgia market is that foreigners cannot purchase or own agricultural land, a nod to the importance of the local, small-scale farming cultures peppered across the country’s regions.

Industry observers note that uruguay’s buying process could not be more straightforward. South America’s second-smallest sovereign country requires no citizenship, visa, or prior approvals. Under Uruguayan law, foreign buyers are given the same rights as citizens and enjoy the benefits of free capital flow. Locals are just as, if not more, tourist-friendly. The country is known for its hospitality, laid-back café culture, and stunning coastal landscapes.

It has been revealed that instead of retiring to Florida, consider this balmy, beautiful Caribbean country—just a four-hour direct flight from the Fresh York area. Like everything else on the island, the real estate laws are relatively relaxed, making buying a house easy-breezy; and you can buy and own property without obtaining residency status or special permissions, as is the case in many other Caribbean islands. “Foreigners can own property outright in the Dominican Republic, with legal protections for foreign investors,” says Mauricio Umansky, CEO and founder of The Agency. One notable consideration is financing: You can certainly get a mortgage in the DR, but it may not be quite as cushy as what you can get in the U.S.—so pay cash if possible.

Great news if you’ve been wanting a more provincial life: Americans face zero restrictions when buying homes in France. The open market allows for statesiders to buy houses, apartments, or plots of land in the city, countryside, and coastal towns in person or remotely without needing citizenship, residency, or even a local visa. However, a purchase does not grant residency, so if you’re hoping to make France your permanent home, you’ll want to apply for a separate long-stay visa and note the Schengen 90-out-of-180-day rule. While buying may be simple, the finances are anything but. Closing fees, including notary fees, typically add seven to ten percent to your purchase. Mortgage rates are also incredibly hard to secure for U.S.-based buyers, thanks to strict debt-to-income caps and FATCA compliance. To simplify the process, many buyers opt to put 20 percent to 40 percent down in cash.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the most American-friendly market, Panama boasts a large English-speaking market, virtually no restrictions on foreign property ownership, and uses the U.S. dollar as legal tender in a vastly affordable market. The Central American nation also offers residency programs like the Friendly Nations Visa, clearing the way legally for residency by investment. In addition to an efficient legal system and reliable market, Panama boasts breathtaking beaches, lush rainforests, and exceptional wildlife.

If you’re hoping for a home in the coffee valleys of Colombia, you’ll need to hire a real estate lawyer before you start scouting for mountain chalets, coffee triangle treehouses, and rainforest retreats. The Caribbean country opts out of standardized agent licensing systems, making legal aid essential to verify title and freedom certificates. While citizenship isn’t required, you will need to secure a tourist visa and Colombian Tax ID to complete your purchase and register for property taxes.

Sources indicate that the buying process in Greece is lengthy, though it is streamlined, with a clear checklist for American buyers to find success in the market. Hiring a local lawyer or notary is a great first step after scouting properties. Not only are they familiar with title checks and contracts, but they can also navigate the intricacies that come with buying in designated border areas or near military zones, which require special clearance for non–EU buyers. While the most popular areas for American buyers, like Athens and Crete, don’t come with heavy legal intricacies, buying any property in Greece will mean securing a Greek Tax Number—a small price to pay for cities with such rich histories and breathtaking seaside views.

According to recent reports, the people in this popular Western European coastal country are famously friendly and inviting, and that extends to real estate. According to Samira Easton, a certified international property specialist with Premier Sotheby’s International Realty, Portugal offers a Golden Visa Program, which makes it simple to buy property and gain residency; clear real estate laws; and a well-established network of English-speaking real estate agents, lawyers, and notaries to help you during the process.

Belize is home to one of the most vibrant, tourist-friendly cultures in Central America, mixing Mayan, Hispanic, Asian, and Creole cultures in its dense rainforests and rolling low plains. Buying here is as easy as it can get, as outright ownership applies to foreigners, and a British-inspired legal system abolishes language barriers and makes contracts easier to understand. Even more, there is no capital gains tax in Belize, and property taxes trend low. The country also boasts vibrant marine life and is home to the world’s second-largest barrier reef.

Sources indicate that spain may have ended its investor visa program in 2025, but the real estate market is still remarkably easy for Americans to navigate. The country currently imposes no restrictions on foreign or nonresident property ownership, but there are a few things you’ll need to procure before you buy, like a Foreigner Identification Number, which is mandatory for taxes. Despite the minor hurdles, the market is booming both on the ground and online. “There are also numerous online resources and property portals available, so it’s easy to find listings and information,” Easton says. This is a boon for those who aren’t able to make the trip over to Europe to house shop in person.Note that buying property does not grant you residency or bypass the country’s 90-day Schengen limit. If you’re hoping to turn your Spanish holiday into your everyday, you’ll have to apply for a separate visa.

Is It Just Us? Or Was 2026 the Year of Whimsy?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One day, you’re listening to The Cheetah Girls soundtrack on the way to school with an armful of Silly Bandz and the next, you’re worried about making rent, hours lost to Google Sheets, and an unexpected medical bill when you still have a $52 request floating in a sea of Venmo transactions.
  • Sources indicate that as for the world we’ve grown into?
  • According to recent reports, “As more of our everyday experiences are shaped by technology and algorithms, people are finding value in things that feel more personal, creative, and unexpected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s face it: Growing up is hard. One day, you’re listening to The Cheetah Girls soundtrack on the way to school with an armful of Silly Bandz and the next, you’re worried about making rent, hours lost to Google Sheets, and an unexpected medical bill when you still have a $52 request floating in a sea of Venmo transactions.

Sources indicate that as for the world we’ve grown into? Nearly two years into Trump’s second presidential term, with AI raising questions about how much of our thinking we’ll hand over to machines, adult life can feel relentlessly optimized and not as chic or shiny as we imagined it as kids. But even if the future feels uncertain, we continue to hope. 2026 has revived the desire to make room for the colorful, playful, and wonderfully impractical again, and that impulse has a name: whimsy.

According to recent reports, “As more of our everyday experiences are shaped by technology and algorithms, people are finding value in things that feel more personal, creative, and unexpected. Inspiration is still incredibly important, but so is the freedom to take what you see and make it your own,” Sydney Stanback, global trends and insights lead at Pinterest, tells Cosmopolitan.

“People are craving more imagination and fun in their everyday lives. There is a real appetite for aesthetics that feel less polished and predictable and more personal, and whimsy gives people room to try something they might not have considered before.”.

And the numbers don’t lie. Pinterest searches for “bedazzling patterns” have increased by a whopping 9,187 percent this year, while “bedazzled phone case” searches are up 8,012 percent. Even “whimsical office outfits” have jumped 885 percent.

In a recent development, from Kylie Jenner’s bejeweled birthday cake and “princess kitty”–themed fete to the deconstructed silhouettes and glittery garments taking over spring/summer 2027 runways, we’re all finding increasingly creative ways to inject personality into our days. In an increasingly automated world, doing things simply because we can is the ultimate act of rebellion. At its core, whimsy is about making magic out of the mundane, whether we’re revisiting childhood obsessions now that we (sort of) have adult money or taking the DIY approach to life to make it more vibrant.

That’s why Cosmopolitan invited 18 colorful, charismatic, and unapologetically authentic tastemakers to share how they’re romanticizing life and embracing their eccentricities. Because to be whimsical is to be human!

Whimsy is having a moment because: You only live once.

The most eccentric thing in my rotation: My grandmother’s ring with engraved details and some of her paint on it.

A childhood obsession I’ve recently revisited: Seashells and rocks.

The most unserious thing I’ve spent money on recently: $12 Swedish fish in the Hamptons. :(.

My most unhinged playlist title: “Vagina Rock”.

The song that never fails to get me on the dance floor: “Stereo Love” by Edward Maya and Vika Jigulina.

The last thing I crafted or DIYed: I made lasagna from scratch a few weekends ago and rolled out all of the pasta sheets with a rolling pin.

The fictional character or public figure who inspires me to embrace whimsy: Every character in SpongeBob.

My favorite way to romanticize life: Staring at a waterfall and/or eating a perfectly cooked steak.

An unexpected thing that brings me an unreasonable amount of joy: Deep cleaning my kitchen and using a Magic Eraser as part of that joyous process.

Whimsy is having a moment because: The clean look is too boring.

The most eccentric thing in my rotation: Of course, NAILS!

A childhood obsession I’ve recently revisited: 3D stickers.

The first time I truly felt free: When I dyed my hair red and went to school.

The artist who never fails to get me on the dance floor: Hatsune Miku.

The fictional character or public figure who inspires me to embrace whimsy: Ai Hoshino from Oshi No Ko.

My favorite way to romanticize life: Listening to music on loud, putting a cute outfit on, and walking around.

An unexpected thing that brings me an unreasonable amount of joy: When I get a compliment.

Occupation: Founder and chief creative officer of Super Smalls.

Whimsy is having a moment because: Everyone deserves to feel like a kid again.

#192262. 10 Sophisticated Gourmand Colognes Perfect for Winter

10 Sophisticated Gourmand Colognes Perfect for Winter

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if there’s one thing you can trust us on, it’s that we’re always keeping our noses on top of the latest fragrance trends.
  • Instead of buttercream and chocolate sauce, think tonka bean and smoke, bitter cacao and rum, toasted sesame and musk, or vanilla and cardamom.
  • When it comes to gourmands, easily one of the most common base notes is vanilla.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if there’s one thing you can trust us on, it’s that we’re always keeping our noses on top of the latest fragrance trends. Right now, one is undeniably taking over, just in time for the cold weather: sophisticated gourmands. If “gourmand” brings to mind the sugary cupcake body sprays your sister bought at the mall as a teenager, you’re not alone in that. But these grown-up “neo-gourmands” take the comforting, familiar sweetness of edible notes and balance them with dry woods, spice, or smoke. The result? A little less syrup, a lot more intrigue and sophistication.

Instead of buttercream and chocolate sauce, think tonka bean and smoke, bitter cacao and rum, toasted sesame and musk, or vanilla and cardamom. Even coffee-scented colognes are taking off right now. There are so many delicious fresh gourmand combinations out there that narrowing them all down to just ten was no easy feat. But we did it, and these are our favorites right now. Consider it your invitation to smell very good (and maybe a little mouthwatering) all winter long.

When it comes to gourmands, easily one of the most common base notes is vanilla. And in fragrance, vanilla definitely does not mean boring—quite the opposite, in fact. Henry Rose’s Dave fragrance combines vanilla and tonka bean at the base for a creamy foundation that’s sweet, but not overwhelmingly sweet.

At the top, we get some nice earthy, slightly spicy notes of tangerine, neroli, and pink pepper, and its heart is softer with florals like orange flower and almond blossom. Base notes of vanilla bean, cocoa, and creamy tonka bean leave you with a smooth, velvety finish.

In a recent development, the great thing about Solférino’s Lumière d’Automne is that it’s both sweet and smoky, but not too much of either. It’s the perfect blend of light gourmand notes (namely vanilla and benzoin) with the hint of smoke that comes from notes of roasted chestnut. The name literally translates to “Autumn Light” and evokes the cozy feeling of wearing a sweater on a chilly day while colorful leaves fall to the ground.

For the past two years, Chai Fleur has been my go-to scent the moment the temperature drops below 50 degrees. I’m not a coffee person, but I do drink a chai latte every day of my life (honestly, I don’t know how I would get through my day without it), and somehow Belnu has captured the scent of chai and turned it into the perfect winter fragrance. It’s sweet and creamy thanks to the base of vanilla and woods, and it has the perfect amount of spice from nutmeg, cinnamon, and green cardamom.

While not technically a gourmand fragrance, Fulton & Roark’s Calle Ocho has notes of bitter chocolate and tonka bean, which give it that velvety-smooth feel that many gourmands have, even if it doesn’t smell quite as sweet as a true gourmand. When blended with cinnamon, rum, florals, smoky tobacco leaf, and musk, the chocolate and tonka bean are transformed into something dark, boozy, sexy, and very sophisticated.

Sometimes, you don’t have to spend more than $100 to smell like you have your life together. In fact, the whole goal of House of Twist is to make affordable fragrances (under $50!) that smell just like your favorite luxury colognes. Liquid Amber No.173 is a spicy gourmand akin to something like Parfums de Marly’s Althaïr (which we also absolutely love), with spicy cinnamon and cardamom, creamy bourbon vanilla, woods, and musks.

Sources indicate that almond is another one of those creamy, nutty scents like pistachio or sesame that thrives in gourmand fragrances. My favorite example of this is Nicolaï Paris’s Macaron Bourbon, an ambery gourmand centered around bitter almond, sweet rum, davana, and patchouli. It’s smooth and creamy without being too rich, so it doesn’t overwhelm you with sweetness. The bitter almond and spices also add an interesting nuttiness to the fragrance, which we love.

According to recent reports, my favorite dessert has got to be a warm sticky toffee pudding with a scoop of vanilla ice cream on top. I never thought there would be a fragrance that captured the warm deliciousness of those exact flavors, but D.S. & Durga, one of our favorite niche fragrance houses, has done just that. Ain’t That Sweet is inspired by a slice of malty date cake and combines notes of cinnamon, date, praline, condensed milk, bourbon vanilla, and nutmeg for an addictive gourmand scent that we’re frankly obsessed with.

You may not expect floral and gourmand notes to go together, but they actually balance each other out quite nicely. In Van Cleef & Arpels’ Orchidée Vanille, the light floral notes of rose and violet lend a nice airiness to the rich gourmand notes of bitter almond, vanilla, and tonka bean. The effect is something sweet but delicate—it’s not the “manliest” of scents in the traditional sense, but we’re very pro-florals when it comes to men’s cologne.

It has been revealed that another one of my favorite newly introduced gourmands that introduced this year is Abel’s Double Scoop, which truly evokes a sweet, nutty ice cream (my favorite kind). But it’s more nuanced than that—it starts off with herbaceous, slightly woody rosemary before revealing the rich notes of toasted black sesame, butterscotch, and vanilla. The dry down is nice and musky, which gives it a sweet but muted lingering aroma.

Finally, if you do want something rich that still feels grown-up and not too sugary, Free Yourself’s Savor is the way to go. It’s a true gourmand with notes of bittersweet chocolate, pistachio, toasted almond, tonka bean, vanilla, and even marshmallow—but it never feels like an overly sweet, juvenile scent in the way you might think marshmallow would lend itself to. That’s because all these rich, creamy, sweet notes are balanced out by plum, rose, and tobacco, which add a more sophisticated twist to the rich gourmand.

Whether you’re curling up by the fire, hosting the family dinner, or bringing dessert to a Friendsgiving, a compliment-worthy manicure is a small comfort when the day gets chaotic. They’ll be passing the cranberry sauce, raising a glass for the toast, clutching a mug of cider—you name it. The good news is that fall offers one of the richest color palettes of the year. Think deep cranberry, burnished copper, mossy olive, and warm cinnamon, all shades that glow against autumn light and flatter nearly every skin tone.

And this season’s nail trends are as varied as the dishes on your table, from minimalist milky neutrals for the understated host to hand-painted leaves and shimmering gold flecks for the one who loves a little drama.

Ahead, check out some Thanksgiving nail ideas to inspire your next set.

Industry observers note that you simply cannot go wrong with brown cat-eye nails. Whether you love a long almond silhouette or prefer a shorter, softer shape, this design feels rich, polished, and effortlessly autumnal.

Plaid nails in autumnal shades bring a fresh, playful spin to a fall manicure.

We love an ombré nail set, and this milky-to-espresso gradient fits right in with the season’s warm neutrals. The soft fade from creamy white to deep, coffee-bean brown feels cozy and sophisticated, like a latte in manicure form.

This butternut-squash yellow adds a fun pop of color to a darker fall palette.

Sources indicate that coffee-glazed nails are the manicure equivalent of a warm mug in your hands. It’s an easy pick for anyone who wants a little shimmer without going full metallic.

Recent findings suggest that can’t pick one fall shade? Wear them all, one on each finger. You’ll be surprised how well they work together.

Rich cherry red nails get a glam upgrade with a delicate gold cuticle line, a classic shade with a jewelry-box finish.

Deep, velvety, and effortlessly chic, this forest-inspired hue pairs beautifully with gold jewelry and cozy knits.

Brown nails with a white chrome topcoat melt into a frosty, taupe-y shade that’s simply stunning.

Rich, moody, and perfectly autumnal, this duo looks like a cranberry-and-herb tablescape on your fingertips.

Tortoiseshell nails are the chicest way to bring warm amber and espresso swirls to your Thanksgiving look.

Sheer, creamy, and effortlessly polished, this minimalist shade pairs with everything from cable-knit sweaters to your fanciest holiday dress.

Delicate, understated, and just a little whimsical, this look pairs a sheer neutral base with one or two hand-painted leaves and a dark French-tip manicure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prince Harry has been back in the UK for some weeks now, and he’s wasted no time in letting everyone know about it, with plenty of public moments including a surprise appearance on This Morning and a family outing to London's Winter Wonderland. But while fans of the Duke of Sussex celebrate his return, the Palace is remarked to be “infuriated” with his recent engagements and, in particular, his request to join the “grid.”.

Speaking to The Express, royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams accused Harry and Meghan Markle of purposely timing their public appointments to take attention away from other members of the royal family.

Industry observers note that “We must assume this has been deliberate. This is deplorable,” the royal expert noted, adding, “[The Palace is] indeed right to be infuriated.”.

But while Fitzwilliams accuses Harry of intentionally scheduling his engagements to outshine his royal counterparts, perhaps it's all just bad timing—which is where the royal “grid” comes into things...

According to recent reports, the royal “grid” is a meticulously organized schedule of the royal family’s engagements and appointments. Although the actual “grid” is not available to the public, fans of the royal family can keep up with their aims via the official website. According to the site, official royal engagements are published up to eight weeks in advance.

According to The Express, Prince Harry has requested that he be added to the royal “grid.” His motive for the move hasn’t been confirmed, but there are of course plenty of theories. Some critics, like royal commentator Fitzwilliams, believe that Harry wants to intentionally create more scheduling conflicts with the other royals. Others take the more agreeable stance that the duke simply wants to avoid any further calendar clashes.

One insider, for example, noted that Harry is “mindful” of his fellow royals and their plans, and tries his best to avoid overlapping with them. “He knows about those things and he is obviously mindful of that as he’s planning his own activities as well,” the source told The Times.

The royal family is split into various households, with Clarence House taking care of King Charles and Queen Camilla and Kensington Palace looking after the Wales family, for example. These households are made up of large teams, covering everything from catering to housekeeping. Also in the royal household are those who proposal and manage the family members’ calendars—these are overseen by private secretaries and diary coordinators.

A previous advertisement for such a job at Kensington Palace said, “The role will be responsible for managing the seamless delivery of multiple complex diaries to ensure the smooth and effective coordination of engagements and events.”.

As for what the role involved? “Compiling and managing coordinated diary updates and weekly overviews; providing regular briefings; communicating diary changes to all key stakeholders, both internally and externally; and carrying out follow-up actions as necessary, as well as ensuring that all events and engagements are accurately recorded,” the listing explained.

Recent findings suggest that “The successful candidate will have a proven ability to manage complex diaries and will have excellent communication skills,” the vacancy ad went on. Being a team player and having a proactive mindset were just some of the other requirements of the role, in addition to maintaining confidentiality and discretion, which the listing described as “paramount.”.

We can't blame you if you're still wanting more from this merry time of year, and we've come up with a solution. There are plenty of beautiful Christmas towns across the country to fill your heart with peace, joy, and nostalgia—you just have to know where to look.

Recent findings suggest that these towns are more than just beautifully decorated—they’re truly immersive, offering experiences from Santa-themed bike rides to orchestrated light highlights and winter bar crawls. Below, we've rounded up the 27 most charming Christmas towns from all over the country, so no matter where you live, you'll be close enough to find a bit of extra cheer this year.

Additional copy by Alyssa Khan.

This picturesque mountain town serves as the perfect holiday backdrop for more reasons than just the ever-present blanket of fluffy white snow. Each year, the valley is transformed into a Christmas town with seasonal theatrical performances, Gunnison’s Night of Lights, a tree lighting ceremony, and even an ice sculpting event.

Sources indicate that ever since the formation of this city on Christmas Eve in 1741, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, has been rooted in the holiday spirit. From Christmas markets to historical tours to horse-drawn carriage rides, there's no doubt this town won't feel magical. And make sure to stop by the historic Sayre Mansion, pictured here, to check out their elegant holiday decor.

Annapolis is known as one of the best cities during the holiday season thanks to its winter weather and historic downtown. If you're lucky enough to visit this Christmas town, make sure you spend time bargain shopping until midnight, checking out the spectacular light display in Sandy Point State Park, and viewing the Yacht Club Light Parade.

Recent findings suggest that chicago is exceptionally beautiful during the Christmas time. From the seemingly endless strings of lights to the Christkindlmarket, which is free to enter and so charming, the Windy City has many offerings during the holiday season, making it one of the best Christmas towns to visit. Plus, you don't want to miss ice skating or any Christmas-themed museum exhibits.

If you want to do something Christmas-y almost every single day of December, then Newport, Rhode Island, might just be the place to go. To create the perfect coastal Christmas, this town offers a month-long celebration that's been going strong for 54 years. From holiday bike rides to Medieval festivals to winter afternoon teas, there's so much to do in this Christmas town.

You'll feel as if you've traveled back to Charles Dickens's time when you walk through Franklin's historic Christmas festival. Characters from A Christmas Carol and Oliver Twist come to life throughout the weekend-long festivities. Roam the Victorian Village and try Victorian-era Christmas treats like sugar plums while listening to carolers.

A classic ski town, Park City offers Christmas markets, festive decorations, and a Christmas Eve parade lit by torches—plus spectacular views of the mountains are around every corner.

In the heart of Virginia horse country, you'll find one of the most festive Christmas towns. Cheer on the town's hunting hounds while sipping hard cider and wander the streets in search of vintage Christmas ornaments.

During Kennebunkport's annual Christmas Prelude, the town puts on a very Upcoming England celebration: You can watch Santa Claus arrive by lobster boat, go on seashore holiday trolley rides, and enjoy wine tastings and lobster bakes. Not to mention, the town is covered in Christmas lights and garlands that make it the perfect festive photo backdrop.

According to recent reports, for a dreamy and unique experience, head to Santa Fe. One of the most anticipated celebrations is the Canyon Road Farolito Walk, which is when thousands of farolitos—luminaries made of paper bags, sand, and tea candles—cast a glow on the gardens and old buildings that line the road. You also can get your white Christmas fix by visiting Ski Santa Fe.

As one of the oldest towns in the country, Portsmouth is a charming New England destination that celebrates the holidays with a Vintage Christmas Celebration. Visit the historic village of Strawberry Banke or wander around the charming shopping districts in this historic Christmas town.

It has been revealed that get a Hallmark movie feel while experiencing a taste of Denmark in California's Solvang village, located in Santa Ynez Valley wine country. The destination hosts Julefest, a month-long holiday celebration with live entertainment, a parade, and a night market.

Koziar's Christmas Village in Bernville is one of the top attractions in Pennsylvania. With more than a million lights adorning buildings, barns, and the landscape—and a reflective lake that doubles the beauty—it's hard to beat the town's display.

This Bavarian-style village is charming any time of year! December festivities include a display of Santa costumes from all around the world, a gingerbread house competition, carolers, and plenty of photo ops.

Recent findings suggest that of course, Newly introduced York City isn't a small Christmas town, but it is extra magical during the holidays. From the massive tree at Rockefeller Center to the various Christmas markets in the city parks with ice skating, shops, and more, you can't beat the Major Apple's holiday spirit.

It has been revealed that nicknamed the Lighted Poinsettia Capital of Texas, this town brings major holiday spirit every year. Visit during December when the lighted trail in Comanche Trail Park is aglow all month long. Check out Hotel Settles for its elegant Art Deco lodging.

Recent findings suggest that during the holiday season, each home in Historic Williamsburg lights one candle, a tradition that dates back to the Revolutionary War era. The cobblestone streets and colonial holiday traditions such as caroling by torchlight make this destination a must, especially for history buffs.

This Christmas town stays decked out year-round, so if you're craving holiday spirit in July, you'll still find candy-cane posts, boughs of holly, and a Santa Claus house with live reindeer!

Christmas without the cold? We've got you covered! In addition to abundant sunshine and festive holiday decor, you'll also have plenty of history to explore in St. Augustine, America's oldest city.

Want to take a ride on the Polar Express? Visit Durango during the holidays. The historic mining town offers a Polar Express–inspired trip that your kiddos will flip over.

It has been revealed that wondering how Taylor Swift feels about the Vanity Fair piece about her? She’s not sweating it. A source tells Page Six that the singer is unfazed by the article, explaining that “Taylor has never pretended to be perfect, but she doesn’t believe a collection of old grievances and unflattering anecdotes defines who she is or what she’s accomplished. To her, it feels like the conclusion was already written and they just went looking for people willing to support it.”.

They add that “At the end of the day, she’s proud of what she’s accomplished and isn’t going to lose sleep over any of this, especially given how the piece has been received by others in the media.”.

According to recent reports, as for Travis Kelce, Page Six’s insider notes that he “is always going to have Taylor’s back. He knows the person she is behind closed doors, and that’s what matters to him. He sees how hard she works, how much she cares about the people in her life and how much of herself she puts into everything she does. He’s incredibly proud of her and isn’t about to let someone else’s perception of who she is change the way he sees her. If anything, he thinks the whole thing says more about the people trying to tear her down than it does about Taylor.”.

Sources indicate that taylor hasn’t spoken out about the article, titled “The Mastermind,” but fans have come to her defense. Meanwhile, there’s a debate in Variety about whether the piece counts as journalism.

Either way, the story has dominated the pop-cultural discourse since its publication on Monday, November 23. Think we can all agree an Ugg collab is the best way to handle this one!

In a recent development, the kitchen has evolved from a hardworking cook space into a multifunctional room for lounging, gathering, and entertaining. So naturally, appliances are changing, too: They need to be as beautiful as they are functional.

Sources indicate that many associate appliances with stainless steel—it has been the go-to choice in kitchens for decades. The material even took center stage in our 1939 Washable House, where it made classic worktables and countertops easier to clean. But today’s design is making room for more colorful choices.

The kitchen designers behind our 2026 Whole Home in Charleston embraced that shift, showing how the room’s most essential appliance—the range—can balance utility with style.

Industry observers note that for the kitchen’s centerpiece, designer Susan Ford of Bennett Hofford chose a La Cornue CornuFé range in Quintessential Teal. White-veined marble, creamy cabinetry, and golden hardware frame the deep blue hue, which continues across the lower cabinets to anchor the design.

The color also plays beautifully against the plush terra-cotta stools lining the island. Designer Chloe Legras of Boxwood Avenue, who designed the adjacent great room, selected the stools and other kitchen accents.

Beyond its color, the range features millwork in mixed metals, giving the traditional detail a futuristic edge and adding character to the small but bespoke space. A Parisian-style range hood with gold details completes the look.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking to elevate your kitchen, take a cue from our Whole Home. This design is bold enough to impress the design-obsessed and practical enough for the bustle of everyday life.

“Bono is usually a man with a lot of ideas,” says photographer/director Anton Corbijn, “so initially we have a conversation and then maybe I make it more theatrical or whatever.”.

Recent findings suggest that that overly casual-sounding process has led to the most extensive collaboration ever between a band and a visual artist. Since their first encounter in 1982, Corbijn has helped establish the evolving public image of U2 across album covers, music videos, and photo shoots for almost 45 years, including the landmark cover of The Joshua Tree, the all-out aesthetic reboot for Achtung Baby, and music videos including “Pride (In the Name of Love)” and “One.” (The partnership is extensively documented in Corbijn’s 2005 book U2&i.) Most recently, they reconnected for a connected pair of surreal and evocative videos—“The Greatest Show on Earth” and “Can’t Stop Us Now”—from U2’s new album Carnaval de Luz, the band’s first full-length release in nine years.

Bono recalls first noticing Corbijn’s work when he was still a teenager, especially a photo of Joy Division that ran on the cover of NME in 1980 following the suicide of lead singer Ian Curtis. “Seeing Anton make these images of these people, they were actual human beings,” he says. “We think from their music that they’re certainly not, but then these images prove that they’re people who lived just across the way. It’s like making movies.”.

In a recent development, indeed, Corbijn has gone on to direct films, including the acclaimed 2007 Ian Curtis biopic Control, as well as doing videos and album covers for Nirvana, Tom Waits, Metallica, the Rolling Stones, and R.E.M. and decades of ongoing work with Depeche Mode.

“It’s difficult for a photographer to shoot bands,” he says, “because bands have an identity, and you need to somehow get that right. It’s very notable that the pictures I do with Depeche Mode don’t look like the pictures I do with U2.”.

It has been revealed that recently, Bono (in New York City) and Corbijn (in Amsterdam) met up on Zoom to discuss their unprecedented alliance, playfully referring to each other as “A” and “B” and recalling shared moments and mutual inspiration. (They also revealed that Corbijn made a film about the American leg of the 2017 Joshua Tree 30th-anniversary tour, which they are planning to bring to local screens during next year’s Carnaval de Luz: The Greatest Show on Earth dates.).

“There are, of course, many occasions where a great artist springs up on their own—a painter, a songwriter, a photographer, a filmmaker, novelist,” notes Bono. “But often there’s some kind of community. U2’s music certainly comes out of community, and Anton is a huge part of our community.”.

This conversation was edited for length and clarity.

Bono: The great stories in songwriting are often unexplained, not resolved. And Anton, your gift to U2 was that you want the emotions to cohere rather than to explain the music. If everything adds up, it adds up to nothing. It’s the thing that you can’t explain that keeps you going back to the work—which sounds like that might be an excuse for laziness, for half-finished lyrics, but I felt over our time together that you finished some of the lyrics for me with your images.

The comedy and the tragedy of “The Greatest Show on Earth” is a real example of that. I hope it’s not too close to the bone with the singer playing the leader of a religious cult and the women doing all the work. But look, anyone who can get the members of U2 to put on beards and look like ZZ Top is some sort of shaman. To do one of your film clips is to risk being very silly—and whilst I don’t have that fear in general, as is obvious from the pratfalls I’ve made in my life and artistic life, the other three members of the band do have a certain amount of self-respect, and so only their faith in you as an artist and trust in you as a friend would have them participate at the level they did.

Recent findings suggest that anton Corbijn: I don’t want to make anybody look silly, but weird is good, and strange, and like you said. I have a very intuitive approach, and we collaborate. Famously, what became the cover of The Joshua Tree was me looking at the desert for a photograph for an album U2 were calling Desert Songs.

Bono: Yeah, yeah, that’s right. Another [potential] title was The Two Americas. But wasn’t it on that shoot we found the title? Via you, and especially the way you pronounced “Yah-shua Tree.” I hope you still find it amusing that we find your Dutch accent amusing.

But as often happens in art, the reason becomes clear years later. That’s the strangest thing—it didn’t start with the Joshua tree; it’s at the end you discovered it. On Carnaval de Luz, we knew from the beginning what we were thinking about, but we discovered it at the very end with the image maker, with the icon maker.

It has been revealed that corbijn: I remember we had a three-day shoot, and we were driving from Reno to Palm Springs, and after the first day, we walked together to the hotel in the desert. And I told you about this tree that I liked so much. I had this landscape camera where the lens moved, so you could get very long shots. I thought it was really nice that you have a tree on the front, and the image goes on to the back, and the band is on the back. So I was talking about that, and I mentioned the name of that tree. And then, the next morning, you came down with the Bible in your hand and mentioned, “It’s got to be The Joshua Tree!”.

It has been revealed that bono: We had no idea that Joshua is the same name as Jesus, Yeshua, and what post-punk band would put an album out called The Jesus Tree? But we forget, because the world is going through some parched times presently, that even though the ’80s seemed to be great for a lot of people—you had the Material Girl and dance music, and Newly introduced York was flying—there was something up in the ’80s. Springsteen would say there was a darkness on the edge of town. And I think for us to dress as pilgrims, as Irish people coming to America, was absurd but actually very effective.

Sources indicate that we were trying to figure out, How do you not look stupid on a magazine cover? How are you to be? I mean, we were in our early 20s, and we were not elegantly wasted, as was kind of the mood of the time—if you’re in a rock ’n’ roll band, you should have the good manners to at least look like you’re about to die any minute. You don’t want to look earnest. And we needed to find our own way of, How do we be ourselves? What masks can we choose to reveal ourselves? What is the iconography of whatever the project is? That naturally led on to Zoo TV and all the various shoots we did for Achtung Baby and Zooropa and all that.

My favorite session of ours, Anton, is when we shot for Pop in Miami. They’re some of my favorite photographs of the band because you seem to photograph what the work is rather than what the people are. So for Pop, you went for bright colors and mischief and charm. Anton, do you remember those sessions in Miami?

Corbijn: Yeah, vividly actually, because you were still recording at the time, in the basement in a hotel. We were young and playful, and so many different options with clothing as well. And we tried funny-looking shots and playful shots, serious stuff as well, but I think after The Joshua Tree, I was attempting to bring more life into the pictures with color use. I also remember you saying that at the time that you liked the colorful stuff I did with Depeche. It was not fresh for me, but we did cross-processing so the color became very vivid, and that’s why Achtung Baby looks so colorful.

It has been revealed that bono: We always live by this sort of modus that the songs will tell us what to do. The songs will tell us how to look, how to behave, what the live show is about, how to dress onstage and sometimes even offstage—and because your thing was, “I’m shooting the song; I’m shooting the material, not you,” I think that really worked for us.

Recent findings suggest that one thing I’d like to ask you, Anton: Would you be comfortable talking about the religiosity of your work? It’s a recurring theme for you, and can you explain a little bit of that?

It has been revealed that corbijn: Not really, actually. I don’t go to church anymore. My father was a pastor, and my grandfather, and all my uncles, and so it sort of made me walk away from it. But I think because I grew up with it, it’s just in my visual language. We grew up next to a cemetery, and maybe that had something to do with it, but the visual iconography, the Christian iconography, is in our society so much that it’s hard to not use it. Sometimes it’s just there—like the first pictures I did with Depeche Mode in ’81, when they were a teeny-tiny pop band, was in this studio in London, and there was this cross with Jesus on it in the garden. So in the photograph, they were like teenybop guys, but still Christ is hanging in the picture.

According to recent reports, bono: Religion has often been such a negative force in the world. It’s very understandable that we would try to avoid the obvious imagery associated with it, but in my life it’s turned into a very positive thing. It’s sort of buoyed me up. But you have it in all your work, despite your attempt to get away from it, I suppose.

Recent findings suggest that corbijn: I was just thinking, in the “One” video, there’s the Father, Son, and the Holy Ghost, and the band, and the woman. It was all in there. I think it’s very nice that I knew your father and you met my father.

Bono: Yes, that’s right. Two powerful men in our lives. But again, your ability to talk people into doing things—you asked my father to stand on a seesaw, and he went along with it, he was fascinated by it. And then you got the four fathers of U2, the fathers and sons.

Industry observers note that corbijn: That was one of my favorite pictures of U2. There’s a lot of depth in it.

Bono: What other favorites do you have, Anton?

Corbijn: Well, I made a book of 500 pages on U2, full of pictures I like. I like some of the photographs we did around Rattle and Hum. That was not a good time for me, but I think there’s some good pictures there. Also on the rooftop in L.A.—I don’t mean the playing one, but the one when we looked at the rooftop, when we discovered it.

According to recent reports, bono: I found this hotel, a real hotel called the Rosslyn Million Dollar Hotel. I was reading Bukowski at the time, listening to Tom Waits, and I walked into this hotel. I couldn’t believe it existed. Eventually I managed to convince Wim Wenders to make a film there. And we so loved the sign, the Million Dollar Hotel, that when we played on that rooftop, we rebuilt the sign.

Industry observers note that corbijn: Yeah but on a much smaller rooftop. I’m in the video, actually. I’m trying to get through the crowd, pointing to the policeman that I have a pass, and he goes, “You go that way!”.

Bono: That poor man, that policeman who pulled the plug. By all accounts, his children tortured him, and he was the most unpopular cop in Los Angeles. He was just doing his job.

Let me see if I one more question for my hero and friend...

According to recent reports, corbijn: I have a question. Why?

As much as we love a latest throw pillow or vase under the Christmas tree, we know that some of the most coveted presents are electronic. So whoever you’re shopping for, from the chronically online teen to the discerning coworker, will appreciate these genius gifts.

Just don’t forget to personalize the item to your recipient. If they have interests such as photography and videography, consider getting them a tripod or GoPro camera so they can document all their action-packed adventures. The nature lover in your life will appreciate a smart bird feeder, and the chef will use the smart stand mixer all the time.

Below, we rounded up dozens of the coolest tech gifts on the market. Of course, we included tested and approved favorites from our very own staff. The technology that changed our lives will make for some super thoughtful gifts.

Industry observers note that the Brick duo is kind of the anti-tech tech gift. If your loved one has been wanting to cut down their screen time, this is the smartest tool to help them do that. It works as a separation between you and your most distracting apps. One that can’t be dismissed without physical interaction. “I keep a Brick at my desk and in my kitchen as barriers to my doomscrolling habit,” Associate Shopping Editor Janae McKenzie says. “But the Brick Night is a real game-changer—it’s Bluetooth location-based, so the moment I cross the threshold into my bedroom, all my social apps are locked, so I actually have to go to sleep at a decent hour.”.

Instead of hardwiring, they use a rechargeable battery pack, so you can display the warm light and vibrant color with no ugly wires in sight. Installation is as easy as attaching a few Command strips.

According to recent reports, the steamer is the new wrinkle-releasing mainstay, leaving the iron in the past. But instead of merely spraying steam, the Nori Cloud Max comes with vacuum technology that pulls the clothes toward the steamer. This smooths out your clothes with way fewer passes.

They work like space-saving bags, but small enough to fit in a carry-on and take on the go. No more calls to the hotel front desk for a vacuum.”.

The easiest way to make your bathroom feel like a spa? Add a towel warmer. Stepping out of the shower, you can retrieve a fluffy towel from this heater to wrap up in, easing the harsh cold of tile floors. It comes with a timer, so you won’t have to worry about leaving it on overnight.

Yes, landlines are cool again. This retro receiver attachment plugs into your phone’s USB-C port, so when you pick up a call, you can have a more tactile experience. It comes with a mic and speaker, so it’s primed for everything from your next Zoom meeting to long-distance catch-up chats.

Tech Report: How to Care for a Thanksgiving Cactus so It Blooms Right on Time

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that want an easy-care plant to brighten your home through fall and winter?
  • Sources indicate that thanksgiving cacti can grow outdoors in USDA Hardiness Zones 10–12, but they’re well suited to indoor life in any climate.
  • Industry observers note that wondering how to help yours thrive?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want an easy-care plant to brighten your home through fall and winter? Skip the usual mums and try a Thanksgiving cactus. Though it’s native to Brazil, this plant looks nothing like a desert cactus: Its flat, toothed stems end in pointed tips, and its vivid tubular flowers usually appear in late November. That timing is how it got its name. It’s related to Easter and Christmas cacti, which flower around their namesake holidays.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving cacti can grow outdoors in USDA Hardiness Zones 10–12, but they’re well suited to indoor life in any climate. Their bright flowers come in colors including red, pink, white, and yellow, adding a cheerful burst of color to a room.

Industry observers note that wondering how to help yours thrive? Here’s what to know about growing and caring for a Thanksgiving cactus.

Industry observers note that the Thanksgiving cactus loves bright spots that aren't in direct sunlight. Too much sun can cause the plant to turn yellow rather than its beautiful green, so keeping it by a north- or east-facing window or even a shady south- or west-facing window is ideal. For your plant to produce the best flowers, it shouldn't receive more than 12 hours of light. It needs the darkness to produce blooms.

All holiday cacti require a bit more magnesium than other houseplants, so finding your Thanksgiving cactus a magnesium-rich fertilizer you can add to a well-draining soil is essential. The Home and Garden Information Center (HGIC) suggests supplementing its water with Epsom salts—try mixing in one teaspoon of Epsom salts per gallon of water. But avoid doing so during the week you add the fertilizer, which you should do once a month. Stop adding fertilizer in the late summer months for better flower production in the fall.

Thanksgiving cacti should be planted in a pot with drainage holes at the bottom since they won't thrive in soggy soil. Consider adding peat moss or sand to the pot to prevent pooling water around the roots. Thanksgiving cacti are root-bound, so there's no need to repot them for about two to three years.

The soil surrounding your Thanksgiving cactus should never be soaking wet or bone dry. However, the soil should be consistently moist and never fully dry to the touch. Holiday cacti are prone to root rot, so standing water is your main enemy. During the hot months, they can stand to be slightly underwatered.

In a recent development, like most tropical plants, Thanksgiving cacti thrive in a humid, warm environment. However, the typical household temperature can keep a cactus very healthy too. The temperature shouldn't get above 80 degrees Fahrenheit or below 55 degrees, though ideally you should keep your cactus between 75 and 80 degrees during the day, according to the University of Wisconsin-Madison's Horticulture Department.

Sources indicate that pruning is an crucial task for plant lovers to keep any houseplant healthy, and Thanksgiving cacti are no different. To promote bud growth, cut the stems in the late spring or early summer, and make sure you have the right gardening tools for the job. Be sure to save the cut stems for propagation too!

In a recent development, if you want more of these tropical cacti around your house, maybe for a huge, flowering centerpiece for the holidays, use cut stems to produce more plants. HGIC suggests using stems with three to five phylloclades (or stem joints) on each to start. Set the segments aside for a day to dry out, then stick them about one inch deep into a pot with moist soil. Do this only in the spring and summer while the plant is actively growing, and avoid doing it in the winter once it has bloomed.

Recent findings suggest that because the Thanksgiving cactus is native to Brazil, you should try to mimic its natural environment as best you can to get it to bloom, which is near the end of the rainy season. The gardening department at Michigan State University Extension explains that for the buds to develop on your indoor plant, Thanksgiving cacti need at least 13 hours of total darkness each day, bright light when they're not covered up or hidden away, and a consistent temperature ranging between 55 and 65 degrees. You should start this process in late September or early October if you want blooms around the holiday season.

Once the plant has flowered for the season, then you can go back to taking care of it the way you normally would with the help of the guidelines written above.

Recent findings suggest that according to PetMD, Thanksgiving cacti are not toxic to dogs and cats, unlike another holiday plant, the poinsettia. However, that doesn't mean you should let your furry friends munch on it. If large amounts are consumed, your pets can experience vomiting, diarrhea, and a decreased appetite.
